newsitem.title: CHINA: S.Korean Red Cross in Beijing for food aid talks.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean Red Cross in Beijing for food aid talks.

text.p: A South Korean Red Cross team arrived in Beijing on Friday for the first talks in almost five years with their counterparts from North Korea, which are aimed at speeding up food aid to the hungry North.
"I expect good results," Lee Byung-woong, secretary-general of the South Korean Red Cross and chief negotiator, said about this weekend's talks on his arrival in the Chinese capital.
South Korea's National Unification Ministry said last month the talks, due to begin on Saturday, would focus on procedures for transporting and distributing food, but not the size or timing of aid.

International aid groups say North Korea, hit by devastating floods for two years in a row, is sliding into famine with reported deaths of children from malnutrition and farmers eating powdered wood to fill out their diet.

North Korea has said its food supplies would run out at the end of April. The U.N. World Food Programme estimated there was only enough food to feed the country until June and then its 24 million people would have to wait for the next harvest in October and November.
A member of the South Korean Red Cross delegation said the group would seek assurances in the talks that food aid would not go to the North Korean army.
The delegation would also discuss the name to be printed on bags containing the food aid for the North with South Korea to demand its name be displayed, another delegation member said.

In Seoul, a South Korean Red Cross official said the South would propose delivering food aid through the Korean border village of Panmunjom, instead of the present methods of using ships or trains through China.
The official, who asked not to be identified, said the South wanted to hand over aid directly to the North instead of through the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies.
"The direct delivery through Panmunjom will quicken relief supplies and cut costs," the official said.
Officials said they did not know how long the talks would last.
The North Korean Red Cross delegation was scheduled to arrive in Beijing on Saturday morning.
The talks have been held up amid bickering between the two sides over where to hold the negotiations. The North insisted on Beijing while the South wanted talks in Panmunjom.
The last inter-Korean Red Cross talks were held in August, 1992 in Panmunjom, the only border crossing point between the two Koreas.
The two nations remain technically at war after their 1950-53 conflict ended in a truce.
The South Korean Red Cross delivered 1,380 tonnes of corn to North Korea by train on Wednesday. The corn, worth 180 million won ($200,000), was donated by a Buddhist group and bought in China.
South Korea's Red Cross also planned to ship 110 tonnes of wheat flour worth 36 million won to the North on Friday. The aid was bought with money raised by a South Korean Christian group.

The World Food Programme has estimated North Korea would need 1.3 million tonnes of additional food to meet its basic needs in 1997 to avert a famine that could turn into "one of the biggest humanitarian disasters of our lifetime".
